network

Abstract
Patentability assessment is the most critical stage of the patent registration process. For an 
invention to be granted a patent, it must meet the patentability criteria of novelty, inven-
tive step, and industrial applicability. Evaluating the novelty and inventive step requires a 
comparison of patent texts in terms of their technical scope. This comparison is conducted 
by experts from authorized patent offices and communicated to applicants through offi-
cial reports. Under the EP and PCT conventions, patentability evaluations are expressed in 
search reports using the categories X, Y, and A. Due to the lengthy and complex structure 
of patent texts, as well as the specialized nature of novelty and inventive step compari-
sons, patentability assessment is a challenging and time-consuming process. Consequently, 
patent registration timelines are extended, and inventions are often submitted prematurely, 
before reaching a patentable level of development. The aim of this study is to address the 
patentability assessment problem from a unique perspective, distinguishing it from other 
semantic similarity tasks, by proposing a semantic similarity model specifically focused on 
patentability evaluation. The proposed model generates patentability text pairs with a focus 
on patent claims and determines the similarity between these pairs using the X, Y, and A 
categorization. The experiment of the proposed model shows that the integration of the 
Siamese network structure with CNN and LSTM deep learning architectures has proven to 
play a highly effective role in achieving accurate results. By utilizing the X, Y, and A codes 
identified by experts in published patent search reports for model training, this study marks 
a significant step forward in solving the patentability assessment problem.

Introduction
With the increasing strategic importance of patent rights in the technology ecosystem, 
the number of patent applications is steadily rising (Bonino et  al., 2010), and the vol-
ume of technical knowledge contained in patent databases has reached immense propor-
tions (Schwander, 2000; Björklund, 1991). Patent documents contain unique, up-to-date 
information that is often unavailable in other sources (Allen & Oppenheim, 1979; Asche, 
2017). R&D activities that do not leverage the insights from patent literature frequently 
fall short of the desired quality (Verhulst, 1997; Atal & Bar, 2010), and many scientific 
publications have used patents as evidence to demonstrate the state of the art (Li et al., 
2013; Chiu & Su, 2014; Yuan & Kumiko, 2014). In addition to serving as a repository 
of technical advancements, patent resources are becoming increasingly attractive for data 
analysis and knowledge extraction (Lin & Chou, 2025). As a large-scale, real-world data-
set, patent information holds significant potential for conducting research and experiments 
aimed at solving a wide range of problems. It can also play a crucial role in addressing key 
challenges in the patenting process. Among these, the most critical aspect to streamline 
is patentability assessment, the evaluation of whether an invention meets the novelty and 
inventive step criteria by comparing it with the most relevant prior art.
In practice, patentability assessment is performed by examiners and they report their 
findings through X, Y, and A codes in search reports under both the European Patent Con-
vention (EPC) and the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) frameworks (Loveniers, 2018). 
The process of conducting patentability assessments and preparing search reports is both 
time-consuming and requires significant expertise, often resulting in delays in the patent 
registration process (Frakes & Wasserman, 2015). Many inventions are submitted for pat-
ent applications without meeting patentability criteria, as inventors are unable to conduct 
patentability assessments themselves. Consequently, these applications fail to secure patent 
protection (Gaudry, 2012). The development of models capable of performing patentability 
assessments using emerging data science and deep learning techniques could play a pivotal 
role in addressing this issue. To design a model capable of effectively handling patentabil-
ity assessment, it is essential to first develop a deep understanding of the unique character-
istics and intrinsic dynamics of the patentability evaluation process itself.
Semantic similarity techniques, which are widely employed to identify the most rele-
vant prior art, form the foundation for developing automated approaches to patentability 
assessment (Shalaby & Zadrozny, 2019). However, the criteria of novelty and inventive 
step introduce domain-specific requirements that go beyond generic similarity measures 
(Schellekens, 2022). It should be clearly emphasized that patentability assessment is funda-
mentally distinct from other forms of semantic comparisons, as it involves not only identi-
fying prior art but also evaluating whether an invention satisfies the novelty and inventive 
step criteria under patent law (Clarke, 2018). That is, identifying a document that is seman-
tically similar to a patent application is not the same as determining whether the application 
satisfies the criteria for patentability. Moreover, patentability evaluation is entirely focused 
on patent claims, as they represent the core of the assessment process. Solely conducting 
semantic similarity comparisons between patent descriptions will not yield accurate results 
for determining patentability. These distinctions illustrate that patentability assessment 
goes far beyond simple semantic similarity; it requires a nuanced, domain-specific evalua-
tion of technical content in light of legal criteria.
Although significant progress has been made in studies focusing on the semantic 
comparison of patents, research specifically aimed at patentability assessment remains

relatively scarce (Kayakökü & Tüfekci, 2025). Existing approaches rarely address inven-
tive step evaluation due to the complexity of capturing nuanced technical contributions 
beyond mere textual similarity. Most studies in the literature focus primarily on identifying 
the most similar patents, while those addressing patentability tend to concentrate solely 
on novelty assessments. Moreover, semantic comparisons of patents are often conducted 
with a focus on the meaning of the entire text, whereas the claims, which constitute the 
core of patentability assessment, remain outside the primary focus of such processes. This 
misalignment limits the applicability of existing semantic models for actual patent exami-
nation practices and has hindered the development of fully automated tools for compre-
hensive patentability assessment. There is an urgent need for semantic similarity models 
capable of evaluating patentability with attention to its domain-specific characteristics, 
encompassing both novelty and inventive step, which remains a critical and underexplored 
gap in the field.
The main contribution of this study is the development of a deep learning-based frame-
work that not only measures semantic similarity but also performs novelty and inventive 
step assessments using real-world patent search report data. The proposed deep learn-
ing architecture is trained on published search reports to identify semantic relationships 
between patent claims and prior art, categorized according to the X, Y, and A classification 
scheme. In this paper first, related work in the field of patent text analysis is reviewed, fol-
lowed by a detailed outline of the proposed model and its patentability assessment capabil-
ities. Subsequently, test results conducted using a patentability dataset, specifically devel-
oped for the testing of the model in the field of electric vehicles, are presented.
Related works
Before reviewing the existing studies on patentability assessment, it is essential to clar-
ify its position within the broader spectrum of research conducted on patent data and to 
accurately define its relationship with other tasks in this domain. Patent data contains both 
structured information such as filing dates, patent classifications, and citation records, and 
unstructured textual content, including descriptions, claims, and abstracts (Abbas et  al., 
2014; Madani & Weber, 2016). Analyses conducted on this multifaceted data often draw 
on a range of techniques, including text mining, natural language processing (NLP), artifi-
cial intelligence (AI), and deep learning (Arts et al., 2018; Chandrasekaran & Mago, 2021).
Beyond patentability assessment, research on patent data encompasses a variety of 
objectives, such as patent classification, clustering, citation analysis, patent network map-
ping, bibliometric evaluation, patent valuation, cross-lingual patent analysis, document 
summarization, technological trend detection, technology forecasting, R&D planning, stra-
tegic planning, competitor profiling, and partner selection (Bonino et al., 2010; Chen et al., 
2015; Chiavetta & Porter, 2013; Rodriguez-Esteban & Bundschus, 2016). While these 
tasks share methodological overlap, particularly in the use of semantic comparison tech-
niques, they differ significantly in their objectives, required domain expertise, and evalua-
tion frameworks (Kayakökü & Akay, 2021; Walter et al., 2017).
Patentability assessment represents the most critical task within the broader category 
of processes that involve examining the semantic similarity of patent texts. Semantic sim-
ilarity methods are widely applied in tasks such as prior art retrieval, patent clustering, 
technology forecasting and so on. Beyond these applications, patentability assessment 
also benefits from semantic comparison techniques; however, it requires the integration of

In the literature, only a limited number of semantic similarity studies have explicitly 
focused on patentability evaluation. Nevertheless, there is a considerable body of work 
in which semantic comparisons between patents have been conducted for other purposes. 
Awareness of these studies is valuable, as methods originally developed for different objec-
tives can inspire or be adapted to semantic comparisons designed specifically for patent-
ability assessment. For this reason, this section first reviews studies directly focused on 
patentability assessment, and then, in a separate subsection, examines works that investi-
gate semantic similarity of patents for other purposes but whose methodologies may be 
transferable to patentability evaluation.
Patentability assessment oriented studies
Patentability assessment refers to the evaluation of whether an invention described in a pat-
ent application meets the legal requirements of novelty and inventive step when compared 
to the prior art. This process is distinct from other forms of semantic comparison, as it goes 
beyond identifying textual similarity to incorporate legal reasoning and domain-specific 
interpretation under patent law. Patent examiners conduct this evaluation during the exami-
nation stage, and only inventions satisfying both criteria are granted patents (Clarke, 2018). 
Importantly, the assessment is centered exclusively on the claims, which define the legal 
scope of protection; semantic similarity between descriptions alone is insufficient for deter-
mining patentability. The text subject to evaluation is therefore the precise content of each 
claim (Lahorte, 2018).
In practice, examiners document their reasoning through formal search reports, which 
classify cited prior art under the European Patent Convention (EPC) and the Patent Coop-
eration Treaty (PCT) frameworks. These reports apply standardized codes: X for docu-
ments that independently anticipate a claim (indicating lack of novelty or inventive step), 
Y for those that preserve novelty but render the claim obvious in combination with other 
Y documents (indicating lack of inventive step), and A for documents that are technically 
relevant but do not affect patentability (Loveniers, 2018). This coding system is a valu-
able but under-utilized resource for developing automated models that emulate examiner 
decision-making.
Despite the centrality of patentability assessment in the patent system, the number of 
studies directly addressing it is relatively small. Many works on patent text analysis avoid 
explicit novelty and inventive step evaluation, likely due to the legal complexity and the 
domain-specific expertise required. For instance, a recent meta-analysis found that only 
about 20% of studies on semantic comparison of patents explicitly reference the concept of 
patentability (Kayakökü & Tüfekci, 2025).
As a widely observed trend in the literature, some studies have focused only on the nov-
elty criterion of patentability. For example, Jeon et al. (2022) vectorized patent documents 
using the Doc2Vec method and applied the Local Outlier Factor algorithm to assess nov-
elty, without addressing the inventive step criterion. Similarly, Chikkamath et al. (2020) 
conducted an empirical study integrating machine learning and natural language process-
ing techniques, comparing the performance of various word embedding models solely 
for novelty detection, again neglecting the inventive step. In another study, Schmitt et al.

One of the few studies that directly focus on patentability assessment is the work by

comparison between claims and cited texts, which is central to novelty and inventive step 
evaluation.
Miyaoka and Akakura (2019) focused on predicting grant or rejection outcomes using 
statistical attributes of patent descriptions through SVM models, without modeling the 
comparative reasoning between examined and cited documents in term of both novelty and 
inventive step. Zhang et al. (2017), on the other hand, developed a retrieval and summari-
zation framework to assist experts in identifying and reviewing relevant prior art but did 
not aim to automatically infer patentability. Schellekens (2022) focused on the inventive 
step criterion and pointed out that evaluating the inventive step is a multidimensional and 
nuanced process, and even AI techniques fall short in demonstrating an inventive approach.
In contrast to these studies, the model proposed in this paper is trained directly on 
expert-assigned X, Y, and A labels extracted from formal patent search reports. It con-
structs semantically aligned text pairs to emulate how examiners compare claim content 
with relevant prior art and uses Siamese neural networks to learn these decision patterns, 
offering a novel and scalable approach to automating patentability assessment.
Semantic comparisons of patent texts for other purposes
Although the following studies were not designed directly for patentability assessment, 
their methodologies for detecting semantic similarity between patent documents can be 
adapted or extended to support novelty and inventive step evaluation.
Text mining and integration of artificial intelligence
For analyzing semantic similarity of patent texts, comparison methods based on set theory, 
where patent documents are defined as clusters of technical concepts (Moehrle, 2010; Park 
et al., 2012), are widely used. Similarly, vector space models, which define patent docu-
ments as vectors based on the technical concepts they contain, are also prevalent (Shahmir-
zadi et al., 2019; Wang & Chen, 2019).
Efforts to improve semantic comparisons have included studies that use the subject-
action-object (SAO) approach to identify technical concepts in patent documents, resulting 
in more accurate semantic comparisons (An et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019; Bergmann 
et  al., 2008). Furthermore, the application of topic modeling techniques such as Latent 
Semantic Analysis (LSA) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) has enhanced the perfor-
mance of semantic comparison methods (Wang & Chen, 2019; Moehrle, 2019; Cvitanić 
et al., 2016).

In addition to corpus-based methods, knowledge-based approaches, which leverage pre-
existing resources such as ontologies, are also employed for the semantic comparison of 
patents (Indukuri et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2015, 2016). Some researchers have gone fur-

patent texts as their source (Jang et al., 2021; Sarica et al., 2020).
Although these methods have yielded significant results in identifying the semantic sim-
ilarities of patent texts, they often fall short when dealing with the complex structure and 
technical terminology of patent documents. However, combining these methods with artifi-
cial intelligence (AI) techniques leads to more effective outcomes (Genin & Zolkin, 2021; 
Villa & Wirz, 2022).
Setchi et al. (2021) emphasized the challenges of patent research and underlined the 
importance of AI techniques in overcoming these difficulties. Integrating AI into patent 
research processes has been particularly successful in determining the patent class of an 
invention and accelerating the process of accessing relevant patent documents.
Deep learning methods
At this point, deep learning algorithms and methods also offer the potential to overcome 
these challenges by delivering surprisingly effective results in data analysis. Through the 
application of deep learning methods in patent analysis, researchers have begun to achieve 
satisfactory results from various perspectives (Aristodemou & Tietze, 2018; Krestel et al., 
2021).
Whalen et al. (2020) noted that both the Word2Vec method and its extension, Doc2Vec, 
are widely used in determining the semantic similarity of patents. A study by Helmers et al. 
(2019) analyzed patent sections such as the description, abstract, and claims separately 
to compare the performance of methods like TF-IDF, Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), 
Word2Vec combined with Bag of Words (BoW) and Doc2Vec, which was more effective 
in analyzing abstracts and claims.
Aras et al. (2018) demonstrated that a Word2Vec model trained specifically on patent 
documents significantly outperforms a general Word2Vec model in measuring patent simi-
larity, as it better captures the unique technical terminology and complex structure of pat-
ent texts. Krishna et al. (2019) utilized deep learning algorithms, including FastText and 
Word2Vec, to identify synonyms and semantically related keywords in patent documents, 
finding that FastText outperformed Word2Vec and resulting in the generation of a dataset 
of synonymous and related terms validated by patent experts.
In another study, Kim et al., (2020a, 2020b) proposed the Sao2Vec method, which vec-
torizes subject-action-object (SAO) features of patent documents using Doc2Vec, achiev-
ing 3% better performance than the classic Doc2Vec and 115% improvement over fre-
quency-based SAO methods.
Lu et  al. (2020) demonstrated that combining Word2Vec with LSTM for context 
embedding and processing the vectors through CNN and MLP significantly improved pat-
ent similarity detection, achieving 94% accuracy compared to 69% with traditional TF-
IDF + Cosine Similarity methods. Kim et al., (2020a, 2020b) demonstrated the efficiency 
of deep learning in patent mining by achieving 97.61% accuracy using a Doc2Vec + DEC 
(Deep Embedding Clustering) method, outperforming other approaches such as Bag of 
Words + K-means (55.47%) and Doc2Vec + GMM (97.55%).
Lei et  al. (2019) highlighted the limitations of traditional vector space models, 
such as Bag of Words and TF-IDF, in capturing semantic relationships and sentence

Transformer‑based and advanced neural approaches
Recent studies highlight the use of Transformer neural networks, such as GPT, GPT-
2, and BERT, in analyzing patent texts, as these architectures outperform other deep 
learning models in understanding and processing textual data, making them highly 
effective for patent analysis (Lee, 2019).
Lee and Hsiang (2020) combined GPT-2 and BERT models for patent similarity 
detection, achieving promising results but highlighting challenges with long patent 
texts. Similarly, Stamatis (2022) achieved promising results in prior art searches by 
employing a two-stage approach combining BM25 and BERT models.
In another study, Li et al. (2023) focused on patent text classification, addressing 
feature extraction challenges by utilizing a dictionary network combined with Word-
2Vec, CNN, LSTM, and BERT models, with BERT achieving the best results.
In a study by Nemani and Vollala (2022), leveraging the capabilities of Transformer 
deep learning networks, such as self-attention and non-sequential data processing, 
DeBERTa variants were employed to detect semantic similarity in patent texts, with 
the DeBERTa-Small model achieving the highest performance.
Despite these advances, most AI-based semantic comparison studies in the patent 
domain remain task-agnostic, meaning they are not explicitly optimized for patentabil-
ity assessment. While they can effectively retrieve similar documents or classify pat-
ents, they typically lack the integration of legal reasoning needed to determine novelty 
and inventive step. As such, their direct applicability to patentability evaluation is lim-
ited without incorporating examiner-driven labeling frameworks such as the X, Y, and 
A codes described in Sect. "Patentability assessment oriented studies".
The approach proposed in this study bridges this gap by combining Siamese neu-
ral networks with a novel, real-world examiner-labeled training dataset specifically 
developed for this purpose, thereby enabling semantic similarity analysis that is legally 
contextualized for patentability assessment. This integration not only leverages the 
strengths of deep learning in handling complex patent language but also ensures that 
the output aligns with established legal standards in patent examination.

Proposed model
The proposed model evaluates the patentability of a given patent document by comparing 
it with other patents within the same technical field. For training the deep learning archi-
tecture, the model leverages published patent search reports from the relevant technical 
domain. These reports serve as a critical resource for determining how the compared patent 
documents influence the patentability of claims, categorized into X, Y, and A classes. The 
overall structure of the model is depicted in Fig. 1, and the subsequent sections will pro-
vide a comprehensive explanation of the model's design phases and implementation.
Generation of the patentability dataset
The model's key feature is its use of domain-specific datasets for patentability analysis, 
generated from published patent search reports containing X, Y, and A labels. A patent 
search report containing the labels X, Y, and A is shown in Fig. 2. These labels reflect pat-
ent examiners' assessments, enabling the generation of specialized training data tailored to 
the technical field of the patent under evaluation. This approach aligns with the principle 
that patent examiners can only assess inventions within their expertise, particularly for the 
inventive step criterion, emphasizing the model's reliance on domain-specific expertise to 
ensure accuracy in patentability decisions.
As seen on Fig. 1 in order to construct the dataset from the search reports, relevant 
documents must be retrieved from patent search engines using keywords and/or IPC/CPC 
classifications aligned with the technical domain of the patent under review. Specifically, 
reports containing X, Y, and A codes-critical for training of deep learning architecture-
are obtained by querying EP (European Patent) or WO (World Intellectual Property Organ-
ization) publications marked with A1 or A3 codes, as these reports include the necessary 
labels. Searches employing "keywords and/or IPC classification" combined with "EP or 
WO" and "A1 or A3" yield the desired results. Extracting essential information such as 
publication numbers, evaluated claim numbers, cited patents, and similarity categories (X, 
Y, A) from these typically PDF reports is achieved using OCR or similar text-recognition 
technologies.
Once this information is extracted, the patent description of the investigated patent can 
be accessed using its publication number, the claim text can be retrieved using the claim 
number, and the description of the cited patent can be obtained using the publication num-
ber of the cited patent. By combining this information with the similarity category (X, Y,

Generation of patentability text pairs
In the design of the model, evaluating entire patent descriptions for patentability would 
demand high computational resources and capacity. To optimize the model's performance 
and efficiency, it is more effective to extract and compare only the most relevant sections 
of these descriptions. This approach aligns with how patent examiners focus on the parts 
of the description that are most closely related to the claims in question, as it is impractical 
for them to read the entire description, especially when it includes details unrelated to the 
claims being assessed for patentability.
The model filters and extracts text pairs based on claimed elements, ensuring relevance 
to patentability. Claims and description paragraphs are vectorized, and the most similar 
paragraphs to the claims are selected from both the examined and cited patents. By com-
paring either the claim to the extracted section of the cited description or sections from

For clarity, throughout this study, the terminology of "claim," "description," and "cited

only their descriptions are considered. This naming convention establishes a clear dis-
tinction between the investigated patent's internal components and the prior art used for 
comparison. Accordingly, in the following sections the constructed patentability text pairs 
may alternatively be called as claim-to-cited description or description-to-cited description 
pairs. This consistent naming convention ensures that the dataset design remains transpar-
ent and unambiguous for interpreting model performance.
Data preparation for deep learning architecture
Once the patentability text pairs are generated, the next step is to prepare them for the deep 
learning architecture. A deliberate choice was made to process patent texts in their original 
form rather than applying heavy preprocessing, such as removing stopwords, filtering ref-
erence numbers, or extracting key terms. This is because in patent claims every word can 
influence the meaning and scope, and empirical testing confirmed that preserving full text 
yields higher accuracy.
The text pairs are transformed into vector representations using advanced embedding 
methods. While traditional approaches like Bag of Words, TF-IDF, LSA, and LDA are 
available, modern neural embeddings such as Word2Vec, Doc2Vec, and FastText offer 
more context-awareness. However, transformer-based models, particularly BERT, have 
shown superior performance in capturing semantic nuances in patent language. In this 
study, the BERT-Base-uncased model is employed for an optimal trade-off between accu-
racy and computational efficiency, with additional experiments conducted using BERT for 
Patents to assess improvements in domain-specific understanding.
The resulting patentability text pairs, derived from the curated patent dataset, are then 
used as the primary training data for the deep learning architecture. Through exposure 
to these labeled pairs, the model learns to determine the degree of semantic similarity 
between compared patent documents within the real-world context of patentability. In prac-
tice, this enables the trained architecture to classify new text pairs into X, Y, or A catego-
ries based on their semantic similarity, thereby emulating the decision-making process of 
patent examiners.
Design and training of the deep learning architecture
A deep learning architecture has been developed to classify patentability text pairs into X, 
Y, or A categories based on their semantic similarity, which is shown Fig. 1. The model 
will be trained on a dataset of tens of thousands of rows, each containing two text pairs and 
their corresponding patentability classification. Two approaches will be tested: (1) a CNN-
based model using vectorized text pairs (e.g., via BERT) and (2) an RNN-based model

processing raw text directly. These alternatives will be compared to determine which offers

CNN architecture
In the CNN-based architecture, input consists of two 1 × 768 vectors from BERT, repre-
senting a pair of patent texts: one related to the current patent document under investiga-
tion and the other corresponding to the cited document. These vectors are either stacked 
into a 2 × 768 matrix for processing by a 2D CNN or directly compared. The CNN applies 
convolutional layers, followed by max pooling, batch normalization for stabilizing, flatten-
ing, and a fully connected layer. A softmax activation then classifies text pairs into three 
categories: X (high similarity, lacks novelty), Y (moderate similarity, inventive step con-
cerns), or A (low similarity, patentable). The model is trained on thousands of labeled pairs 
to predict the X, Y, or A category for new patent text pairs. The overall design of the CNN 
model is illustrated in Fig. 3.
Siamese CNN architecture
In the second approach, a Siamese network with twin 1D CNNs processes the two 1 × 768 
BERT-generated vectors separately. Sharing identical weights and structure, the twin 
CNNs independently extract features from each input. Each branch employs convolutional 
and pooling operations similar to those in the CNN model described in Sect. 3.4.1, but 
applied independently to each input vector. The extracted feature representations are then 
compared by computing the absolute difference between them using a Lambda layer, which 
serves as the similarity measure. The overall design of the Siamese CNN model is illus-
trated in Fig. 4.
This symmetric design ensures that the model captures nuanced relationships between 
patent texts, making it particularly effective for comparing claims and descriptions with-
out combining the vectors into a matrix, as in the first method. The key methodological 
distinction lies in the parallel processing branches and the explicit distance calculation at 
the final stage. During testing, the Siamese CNN demonstrated superior performance over 
the 2D CNN in determining patentability, highlighting its ability to independently model 
and compare separate patent vectors more effectively. Based on these results, further opti-
mization of the Siamese architecture will involve fine-tuning hyperparameters to enhance 
performance.

Siamese LSTM architecture
The third approach leverages an RNN-based method, specifically a Siamese LSTM archi-
tecture, to process patent texts directly without relying solely on fixed-size embeddings. 
Each input text is represented through an embedding layer and then passed to LSTM units 
that capture sequential dependencies across words. To mitigate overfitting, dropout regu-
larization is applied after the LSTM layer, followed by dense projections for feature extrac-
tion. The outputs of the twin networks, which share weights, are compared using a distance 
function implemented via a Lambda layer, and the resulting vector is classified into the X, 
Y, or A categories through a softmax activation layer. This methodological design enables 
the model to capture temporal and contextual patterns in the text, providing an alternative

Vectorization and comparison of patent texts
After constructing the patentability dataset, a series of preliminary experiments were con-
ducted on a limited subset of 15 patents to evaluate alternative approaches for representing 
and comparing patent texts. These initial tests employed the Doc2Vec method combined 
with cosine similarity to determine whether semantically related patents could be identi-
fied and distinguished from unrelated ones. The results indicated that while Doc2Vec cap-
tured general thematic relationships-such as differentiating patents from unrelated techni-
cal fields-it was unable to reflect the expert-defined X, Y, and A classifications used in 
patentability assessments.
Following this, the BERT model was tested for its ability to generate more context-
aware embeddings of patent text. BERT demonstrated superior performance in captur-
ing the semantic alignment between a claim and its corresponding description, as well as 
between claims and cited documents. However, even BERT, when applied solely with sim-
ilarity metrics like cosine distance, proved inadequate for reliably predicting patentability 
categories. These findings reinforced that unsupervised similarity-based methods alone are 
insufficient to model the complex legal and technical reasoning involved in patentability 
evaluations.
Based on these insights, BERT was selected as the core text embedding technique for 
the study-not as a standalone classifier, but as the input layer for a supervised deep learn-
ing architecture trained on real-world, expert-labeled patentability outcomes. The full 
methodology and results of these early embedding comparisons are presented in Appendix 
A, while the main model development builds upon the strengths of BERT within a neural 
classification framework.

In constructing the training dataset, the concept of patentability text pairs was intro-
duced to emulate how expert patent examiners evaluate novelty and inventive step. Rather 
than analyzing full documents, examiners typically focus on the first independent claim 
and compare it with the most relevant sections of the cited patent's description. Based on 
this approach, two types of semantically meaningful text pairs were constructed: (1) the 
first independent claim of the investigated patent paired with the most relevant cited para-
graphs, and (2) a reconstructed segment from the investigated patent's own description-
designed to reflect the scope of the first claim in another way-paired with the relevant 
cited paragraphs. The methodology for identifying these relevant segments is described in 
Sect. "Generation of patentability text pairs".
Therefore the cleaned dataset of 17,757 rows served as the basis for generating two 
types of patentability text pairs used to train the deep learning models. Patentability can 
be decided by comparing the investigated claim with the cited description segment, or by 
comparing the relevant segment of the investigated description with the cited description 
segment. Both types of text pairs have been generated in a way that is conducive to learn-
ing patentability decisions. As a result, from the cleaned dataset, we have obtained two 
different text pairs and their corresponding patentability decisions, generating a 35,000-
row training dataset that can be used to train the deep learning architecture. The text pairs 
generated as described above, along with their BERT vectors and the category information 
indicating the similarity, were obtained as training and test data as follows:
The inclusion of both types of text pairs in the training dataset serves to support the 
model in learning how patent examiners conduct nuanced comparisons. Each pairing type 
offers a complementary view of the claim scope and its relation to prior art. Their com-
bined use is intended to enrich the model's training by providing semantically diverse yet 
contextually aligned examples. More importantly, this curated dataset is used consistently 
across all deep learning architectures evaluated in this study. This ensures that performance 
differences can be attributed to model design rather than variations in training data. The 
primary aim of this dual pairing strategy is not to claim definitive performance gains, but 
to establish a standardized basis for fair and meaningful comparisons between alternative 
deep learning approaches, with the goal of proposing an effective model for patentability 
assessment.
Although the input features for the model are based on patent text segments, the classifi-

using expert-labeled patent search reports, in which domain professionals assign X, Y, or 
A categories after considering novelty and inventive step criteria. These labels inherently 
reflect the technical and legal reasoning of patent examiners. As such, the model learns 
to approximate expert-level assessments based on real-world decision patterns, rather than 
relying solely on textual closeness.

The performance of each model was compared using identical training and test datasets 
comprising 35,000 patentability text pairs. These pairs were generated using two strategies: 
(1) pairing the first independent claim with relevant cited paragraphs and (2) pairing 
reconstructed description segments (representing the claim's protection scope) with cited

differences stemmed from the model architectures and not the input data. It should also be 
noted that the inclusion of both types of text pairs within the same training dataset, while 
beneficial for exposing the model to diverse representations of patentability reasoning, 
may introduce a degree of semantic overlap that could potentially reduce the model's 
generalization capacity in broader applications. Therefore, the results should be interpreted 
primarily as relative performance comparisons between model architectures, with the 
goal of uncovering meaningful insights that contribute to the development of an effective 
patentability assessment model.
The baseline CNN architecture reached a test accuracy of 0.577, with a weighted 
F1-score of 0.58. While acceptable as a benchmark, the model exhibited signs of overfit-
ting in later epochs, with training accuracy continuing to rise while validation accuracy 
stagnated. Furthermore, the recall value for the Y category remained relatively low, indi-
cating difficulty in distinguishing semantically similar categories such as X and Y. This 
suggests that the architecture struggles to capture the nuanced distinctions required in 
patentability assessment.
In contrast, the Siamese CNN architecture achieved a test accuracy of 0.636 and a 
weighted F1-score of 0.63. The improvement reflects the model's better capacity to learn 
comparative relationships rather than relying solely on single input representations. Moreo-
ver, additional architectural tuning (e.g., increasing convolutional depth to 5 layers, using 
BERT for Patents embeddings) further enhanced performance to 0.73 accuracy. This shows 
that Siamese CNNs benefit significantly from well-prepared semantic embeddings.
The Siamese LSTM model, unlike the CNN variants, was trained using raw text as 
input. With an embedding layer trained on the corpus and a 64-unit LSTM on each side of 
the Siamese structure, this model reached a test accuracy of 0.777 and a weighted F1-score 
of 0.78, outperforming all other configurations. While the LSTM-based model had a much 
longer training time due to sequential processing and heavier computational cost, it dem-
onstrated superior generalization, particularly in distinguishing subtle differences between 
categories X and Y. This suggests that LSTM-based models may better capture contextual 
nuance in unstructured patent text, especially when pretrained embeddings are not avail-
able or when raw syntax and sequential structure carry important meaning.

Conclusions and future work
The model developed in this study and the findings obtained provide a significant contri-
bution to addressing the patentability assessment problem. It has been demonstrated that 
designing a model that specifically addresses patentability evaluation-distinct from other 
semantic comparison tasks-by focusing on the criteria of novelty and inventive step is 
crucial for meeting the needs in this field. While the model's performance in achieving X, 
Y, and A categorization is not yet at the desired level, it represents an important starting 
point.
This study also highlights the critical value of published patent search reports as a 
resource for research in patentability assessment and natural language processing. These 
publicly accessible reports, free from ethical concerns, offer a robust dataset that can be 
utilized for various research purposes across different technical fields. As mentioned in the 
testing phase of this study, the patentability dataset developed for electric cars and shared 
in JSON format is a valuable resource that many researchers can benefit from. This dataset 
is not only a significant resource for semantic analysis but also provides important opportu-
nities for researchers working in technology management.
A significant development in this study is the filtering of long patent texts to extract only 
the sections that directly impact patentability decisions, which leads to two highly efficient 
text inputs for the model. It would be extremely difficult to make a patentability comparison

Scientometrics (2025) 130:5401-5440
using only the abstracts, claims, or descriptions of patent applications. Therefore, the 
approach of filtering text specifically for this decision has become a strength of the study. 
Furthermore, defining the claim under scrutiny as the filtering criterion aligns the design 
closely with real-world patent research, as patent examiners also evaluate the parts of the 
description that are most relevant to the claim when making patentability decisions.
The combination of the text pairs approach with the power of Siamese deep learning 
architecture and using these text pairs as input for Siamese networks, greatly enhanced the 
model's ability to make accurate decisions. With Siamese networks, it is possible to work 
with 1D inputs, reducing the computational resources required for handling multidimen-
sional matrices and improving performance.
Although the findings presented in this study have made significant progress in solving 
the patentability problem, it is clear that there is still much work to be done in this area. 
To facilitate more efficient and faster progress in future studies, some recommendations 
should be made.
First, future studies should focus on improving the methods used to obtain patentability 
text pairs. While comparing the vectors of claims and paragraphs is a good starting point, 
efforts should be made to generate text pairs that better reflect the patentability evaluation 
with more accurate and concise texts. The more precise and specific the text pairs are, the 
higher the prediction accuracy will be.
Future studies should also explore the impact of different text pairing strategies for train-
ing dataset construction on model performance. Although the curated dataset constructed 
using two types of text pairs in this work enables meaningful comparisons between deep 
learning architectures, further experimentation is needed to assess how various approaches 
influence the model's absolute accuracy in patentability classification. Understanding these 
effects is essential to strengthen the generalizability and robustness of future models. While 
the current work presents an encouraging and concrete step toward tackling the challenging 
task of patentability assessment, it also highlights the complexity of the problem and the 
need for continued advancements in this field.
Besides, the impact of class imbalance on model performance warrants further inves-
tigation in future studies. To evaluate the robustness of patentability assessment models 
under more controlled conditions, stratified sampling strategies or synthetic balancing 
techniques may be employed. However, it is essential to preserve the integrity of expert-
derived labels during such preprocessing to ensure consistency with real-world decision-
making dynamics in patent examination.
In the future, more advanced models can be integrated into the decision-making mod-
ule, making the design flexible and adaptable to new developments. Another flexible fea-
ture of the design is the ability to generate alternative text pairs. When generating patent-
ability text pairs, the deep learning architecture evaluates the texts obtained from different 
sections of the description separately and presents any X or Y decision to the user. This 
feature helps to ensure that documents with X or Y concerns are not overlooked.
As noted in the testing phase, the tests were limited to the first claims in the dataset. 
Each application in the dataset contains many different claims, most of which are depend-
ent on the first claim or subsequent claims. Future work could involve modeling these 
dependencies and incorporating the semantic analysis and generation of patentability 
text pairs for all claims, which would allow for even more patentability-related data to be 
produced.
Another important direction for future work involves integrating a prior art retrieval 
component into the system. Although the current study does not address the retrieval stage 
explicitly, this step is often more straightforward in real-world scenarios, where researchers

Scientometrics (2025) 130:5401-5440 
can generate candidate sets of related documents using basic keyword and classification-
based searches through public or commercial patent databases. The real challenge lies in 
the accurate evaluation of these documents for patentability-specifically, determining 
novelty and inventive step-which is the primary focus of this study. The proposed 
model, trained on expert-annotated patent search reports, enables automatic classification 
of such documents into X, Y, or A categories once they have been retrieved. Therefore, 
the model offers an operational solution to the most expertise-intensive part of the 
patentability assessment process. In future implementations, retrieval mechanisms based 
on semantic similarity and dense vector search can be incorporated to complete the end-to-
end automation of the patentability evaluation pipeline, provided that access to full-scale 
international patent databases is made available.
In conclusion, the findings from this study represent a significant contribution to solving 
the patentability detection problem, a critical challenge in the field. The results also show 
that much more work is needed to fully solve this problem. Since patentability evaluation is 
a unique process shaped by patent terminology and legal regulations, future studies in this 
field should be specifically designed to address patentability. This study has outlined the 
unique characteristics of patentability and demonstrated that progress can be made in solv-
ing this difficult problem with patentability-focused designs.
As deep learning, natural language processing, and semantic analysis methods continue 
to advance, their capabilities must be rapidly applied to patent documents and databases. It 
is clear that expertise in the patent system is also required to achieve this. Progress in this 
area will not be possible without combining patent knowledge with data science. Encour-
aging data scientists to work in the patent system and encouraging patent experts to explore 
data science will open the door to significant developments in the field of technology and 
innovation.
